subject: philosophy
title: Socratic questioning
objective: Find what a sequence of questions can—and cannot—establish.

lesson.opening: INTERPRETATION: Socratic examination, often called elenchus, tests a respondent’s commitments through questions. Scholars dispute whether it primarily refutes a thesis, exposes inconsistency, or also establishes positive ethical knowledge.

sections.heading: Examination rather than humiliation
sections.body:
Asking many questions is not yet an examination of an argument. A productive sequence identifies a claim, clarifies its meaning, and checks it against other commitments. “What do you mean by courage?” seeks an account; “Can retreat ever be courageous?” tests that account against a case.

Suppose someone says courage means never retreating, then agrees that a tactical retreat can protect others at great personal risk and be courageous. The commitments conflict. This does not by itself tell us which to abandon. It supplies a reason to revise at least one or explain a relevant distinction.

An examination is strongest when the respondent understands the commitments and the proposed case. Ambiguous wording, pressure, or a false dilemma can manufacture apparent contradiction. A fair questioner gives the other person space to clarify rather than treating every hesitation as defeat.

The passage records a portrait of persistent examination about virtue. The method illustrated in our exercise is an editorial reconstruction, not a transcript of a single historical conversation.

sections.heading: Reconstructing the argument
sections.body: Claiming to care about virtue is not the same as showing understanding or living accordingly. Socratic questioning presses the relation between a person’s professed commitment and their other judgments. What the method ultimately proves remains an interpretive question.

sections.heading: A serious objection
sections.body: A critic objects that inconsistency among commitments does not identify the false one. A careful defender should concede that limited result and explain how further inquiry can assess the alternatives.

activities.prompt: Why does the portrayed Socrates continue asking?
choices: A declaration of caring does not settle whether the person’s other commitments support it.

items: Ask what the person means by courage.
Confirm that their account rules out every retreat.
Test a retreat undertaken to protect others.
Ask whether the definition or another commitment needs revision.

activities.prompt: If a person’s accepted claims are inconsistent, what has been established?
choices: Every belief they hold is false.
At least one commitment must be revised or clarified.
The opposite of the opening claim must be true.

activities.prompt: A colleague changes “never” to “usually” after a difficult case. What should you do?
choices: Examine whether the qualification is principled and resolves the difficulty.

activities.prompt: Which reply addresses the critic’s limitation objection?
choices: Admit that exposing inconsistency is a limited result, then assess the competing commitments.
Say the critic is afraid of questions.
Claim that every contradiction proves the examiner right.

activities.prompt: Which most undermines a fair examination?
choices: Letting the respondent revise a claim.
Switching the meaning of a key word without acknowledging it.
A family of question-driven examinations of commitments.
A guarantee that the examiner knows everything.

activities.prompt: Create three fair questions testing “loyalty means always agreeing with a friend.” Do not simply insult or trap the respondent.
activities.context: And if the person with whom I am arguing, says: Yes, but I do care; then I do not leave him or let him go at once; but I proceed to interrogate and examine and cross-examine him, and if I think that he has no virtue in him, but only says that he has, I reproach him with undervaluing the greater, and overvaluing the less.
rubric: I ask for or clarify the definition.
I introduce a relevant case of principled disagreement.
I allow revision and do not pretend inconsistency alone proves my full theory.
